(p-426) Sūrat al-Ḥajj is Makkī, and it has seventy-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord.﴾ He commanded the children of Adam to have taqwā (God-consciousness, piety), then gave the reason for its obligation upon them by mentioning the Hour (al-sāʿah), and described it with the most terrifying description in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ This is so that they may look at that description with their insight and picture it with their intellects, until they preserve their own selves and spare them from the hardships of that Day, by complying with what their Lord commanded them of wrapping themselves in the garment of taqwā, which secures them from those terrors. Zalzalah (zalzalah, violent shaking) means intense agitation and disturbance. The idafah (genitive construction) of zalzalah to al-sāʿah is the idafah of the verbal noun to its agent, as if the Hour itself is what shakes the earth, by way of metaphor in the sense of attribution (al-majāz al-ḥukmī); or it is an idafah to the time (al-ẓarf), because the convulsion occurs within it, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, the scheming of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33]. Its time will be the Day of Resurrection, or at the rising of the sun from its west. There is no proof in it for the Muʿtazilah regarding calling the non-existent "a thing" (shayʾ), for this is a name for it in the state of its existence.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 2:

The phrase ﴿the day you see it﴾ is in the accusative, meaning "the earthquake" or "the Hour," and it is governed by the verb ﴿will be distracted﴾, that is, ﴿taghfulu﴾ (to be heedless). Al-dhuhul (distraction) means heedlessness. ﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾, meaning from her nursing, or from the one she nursed, which is the infant. It was said that the phrase uses "nursing mother" (murdi'a) to indicate that when that terror occurs, she has already put her breast to the suckling infant and then pulls him away from her mouth because of the bewilderment that overtakes her. The murdi'a (nursing mother) is the one who is in the act of nursing, with her breast in the child's mouth, whereas the mu'dir (one who nurses) is the one whose nature is to nurse, even if she is not actually nursing at the time of the description. ﴿And every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾, that is, every woman with child, ﴿her burden﴾, meaning her offspring, before its completion. On the authority of al-Hasan: the nursing mother will be distracted from her child without weaning, and the pregnant woman will drop what is in her womb before its full term. ﴿And you see the people﴾, O observer, ﴿as drunk﴾, by way of comparison, when they witness the carpet of majesty, the sovereignty of might, and the canopy of greatness, until every prophet says, "Myself, myself." ﴿Yet they are not drunk﴾ in reality. ﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe﴾. Thus the fear of Allah's punishment is what took away their minds and reduced them to a state resembling that of one whose intoxication has taken away his reason. And on the authority of al-Hasan: "you see the people drunk" from fear, "and they are not drunk" from wine. "Sukra" in both places is read with imala by Hamza and Ali, and it is like ʿatshā in ʿatshān. It is narrated that the two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited them, and we did not see anyone weeping more than on that night.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 22, verse 3:

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 8] concerning the religion of Allah, ﴿without knowledge﴾. Here "without knowledge" (*bi-ghayr 'ilm*) is a *hal* (a circumstantial accusative, a grammatical state describing the subject at the time of the action). It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a contentious debater and used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," "the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients," and "Allah is not able to bring back to life those who have decayed." Alternatively, the verse is general, covering everyone who disputes about the religion out of desire. ﴿And follows﴾ in this ﴿every rebellious devil﴾, one who is defiant and persistent in evil. There is no pause (*waqf*) at *Marid* (*marid*, "rebellious"), because what follows it is its description (*sifa*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 4:

﴿It was decreed for him﴾ that he [i.e., Satan] would be a judge over the devil, ﴿that he will lead him astray﴾ from the right path, ﴿and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾, the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the fa' in "fa-annahu" is for conjunction (al-'atf), and "anna" is repeated for emphasis (al-ta'kid). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) refuted him and said: if "man" is conditional (li-l-shart), then the fa' has entered upon the response of the condition (jaza' al-shart); and if it means "alladhi" (who), then the fa' has entered upon the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtada'), and the estimate is "fa-al-amr annahu yudilluhu" (so the matter is that he leads him astray). He said: conjunction and emphasis occur only after the completion of the first clause. The meaning is: it was decreed upon the devil that he would lead astray whoever follows him and guide him to the Fire.

Then He established the proof against those who deny the resurrection, saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection﴾ — meaning: if you doubt the resurrection, then what removes your doubt is that you look at your own beginning, for you were, at the start, dust and water, and the only cause of your denial of resurrection is this, namely the transformation of creation into dust and water. ﴿Indeed We created you﴾ — that is, your father — ﴿from dust, then﴾ you were created ﴿from a drop [of semen], then from a clinging clot﴾ — that is, a piece of congealed blood — ﴿then from a lump of flesh﴾ — that is, a small piece of flesh, the size of what can be chewed — ﴿formed and unformed﴾. The "formed" (mukhallaqah) is the shaped and smooth one, free from deficiency and defect. It is as if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates the lumps differing from one another: some of them are complete in form, smooth of defects, and others are the opposite of that. Following this difference is the difference among people in their creation, their forms, their height and shortness, their completeness and deficiency. We have only moved you from one state to another and from one form to another ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾ — through this gradual process — the perfection of Our power and Our wisdom, and that He who is able to create man from dust first, then from a drop second, with no affinity between dust and water, and who is able to make the drop a clot, the clot a lump, and the lump bones, is able to restore what He originated.

﴿And We cause to remain﴾ — with the nominative reading according to those other than al-Mufaddal, it is a new sentence after a pause, meaning: We establish — ﴿in the wombs whatever We will﴾ — its remaining — ﴿for an appointed term﴾, that is, the time of birth. And whatever We do not will to remain, that is, the wombs expel it. ﴿Then We bring you out﴾ from the womb ﴿as infants﴾ — a circumstantial state, and it is meant as a collective noun, which is why it is not pluralized; or it is meant as: then We bring out each one of you as an infant. ﴿Then that you may reach your maturity﴾ — then We raise you so that you reach ﴿your full strength﴾, the perfection of your intellect and your power. It is one of the plural forms for which no singular is used (for it is said "ashuddun" with no singular in use). ﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾ — upon reaching full strength, or before it; and among you is one who is returned — ﴿and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, the lowest of it, meaning senility and dotage — ﴿so that he knows, after knowing, nothing﴾; that is, so that he no longer knows anything of what he used to know, or so that he gains no knowledge and forgets what he once knew.

Then He mentioned another proof for resurrection, saying: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾ — dead and dry — ﴿but when We send down water upon it, it stirs﴾ — it moves with vegetation — ﴿and swells and grows﴾ and is puffed up. In one reading (where he was), "warabat" (it grew) — increases, rises ﴿and makes grow from every kind of﴾ pair, a species, ﴿beautiful﴾, good, pleasing to those who look upon it.

That is (ذَلِكَ), a subject whose predicate is ﴿because Allah is the Truth﴾. That is: what We have mentioned, namely the creation of the children of Adam and the reviving of the earth, together with the various kinds of wisdom contained within that, is accomplished by this, namely that Allah is the Truth, i.e. the One whose existence is established. ﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾, just as He revived the earth, ﴿and that He is Able over everything﴾, i.e. Powerful.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 7:

﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that Allah will raise those who are in the graves.﴾ That is: He is All-Wise, who does not break His promise, and He has promised the Hour and the Resurrection, so He must fulfill what He has promised.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 8:

﴿And among mankind is one who disputes concerning Allah﴾ regarding His attributes, describing Him by what is not His attribute. It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. ﴿without knowledge﴾ that is necessary (ḍarūrī) knowledge, ﴿nor guidance﴾ that is, acquired through reasoning (istidlālī), because it leads to knowledge, ﴿nor a book giving light﴾ that is, revelation. Knowledge for a human being comes from one of these three sources.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 9:

﴿Turning his side away (thāniya ʿiṭfih)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: twisting his neck away from obedience to God out of arrogance and conceit. (p-430) ﴿So that he may lead astray﴾ (li-yuḍilla) is a causal clause (taʿlīl) for the disputing. Makkī and Abū ʿAmr read it as "li-yaḍilla" (with a fatḥa on the yāʾ). ﴿from the way of God﴾, meaning His religion. ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾, that is, being killed on the Day of Badr. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning Fire﴾, meaning: the punishment of both abodes has been gathered for him.

That is (the cause of) your punishment in both abodes: what your own soul has sent forward of disbelief and denial. He referred to it by the hand, because the hand is the instrument of earning. ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ So He does not seize anyone without a sin, nor for the sin of another. It is conjoined to "bi-ma" (by what), meaning: and that Allah... The word ẓallām (one who does great injustice) is mentioned in the intensive form because it is paired with the plural word ʿabīd (servants). Also, even a little injustice from Him, with His knowledge of its ugliness and His independence (from it), is like much of it from us.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 11:

﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge (ḥarf)﴾: on an edge of the religion, not in its center and heart. This is a parable for their being in unease and turmoil regarding their religion, not in tranquility and assurance. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: wavering.

﴿If good befalls him﴾: health in his body and abundance in his livelihood, ﴿he is content (iṭmaʾanna)﴾: he is calm and settled ﴿by it﴾: by the good that has befallen him, or by the religion, so he worships Allah. ﴿But if a trial (fitna) befalls him﴾: evil and affliction in his body and constriction in his livelihood, ﴿he turns about on his face (inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi)﴾: on his direction, that is, he apostatizes (irtadda) and returns to disbelief, like one who is on the edge of the army: if he senses victory and booty, he settles and is content; otherwise he flees and flies off on his face.

They said: it was revealed concerning Bedouin (aʿārīb) who came to Medina as emigrants. One of them, when his body was healthy, his mare foaled a sound foal, and his wife bore a sound boy, and his property and livestock increased, would say: "I have not met with anything but good since I entered this religion of mine," and he would be content. But if the matter was otherwise, he would say: "I have met with nothing but evil," and he would turn away from his religion.

﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter (khasira al-dunyā wal-ākhira)﴾: this is a circumstantial clause, and it is with a implied (muqaddara) element. Its evidence is the reading of Rawh and Zayd: "khāsiran al-dunyā wal-ākhirata." The loss in this world is by being killed in it, and in the Hereafter by abiding forever in the Fire. (p-431) ﴿That﴾: that is, the loss of both abodes, ﴿is the manifest loss (al-khusrān al-mubīn)﴾: the clear loss that is hidden from no one.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 12:**

﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him.﴾ He means: the idol, for after apostasy (ridda) he does likewise. ﴿That which does not harm him﴾ if he does not worship it, ﴿and that which does not benefit him﴾ if he worships it. ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾ away from the right course.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 13:

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. The difficulty is that He, exalted is He, negated harm and benefit from the idols before this verse, and affirmed them for them here. The answer is that when the meaning is understood, this suspicion goes away. That is because God, exalted is He, made the unbeliever look foolish by [describing him as] worshipping an inanimate object that possesses neither harm nor benefit, while he believes in it that it benefits him. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this unbeliever will say, with calling out and shouting, when he sees the harm he suffers from the idols and sees no trace of intercession from them: ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ ﴿Surely wretched is the patron, and surely wretched is the companion﴾. That is, ﴿the patron﴾ means the helper, and ﴿the companion﴾ means the associate. He repeated "yad'u" (he calls upon) as if he had said: he calls upon, he calls upon, apart from God, that which does not harm him and does not benefit him. Then He said: ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾, that is, by his being worshipped, [it is] nearer to harm, than [it is] to benefit by his being an intercessor.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ This is a promise for those who worship Allah in every state, not for those who worship Allah "on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 15:**

﴿Whoever thought that Allah would never help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾. The meaning is: Allah is the helper of His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter, so whoever among his enemies thinks otherwise, ﴿then let him stretch out a rope﴾, a cord, ﴿to the sky﴾, to the ceiling of his house, ﴿then let him cut it off﴾, meaning let him hang himself with it. Hanging oneself (al-ikhtinaq) is called "cutting off" because the one who hangs himself cuts off his breath by blocking its passages. With the vowel of the lam kasra (لِيَقْطَعْ), it is read by the Basran and Syrian readers. ﴿Then let him see (p-٤٣٢) whether his scheme will remove what enrages him﴾, meaning what enrages him, or, with ما as a masdariyya (a particle that, with the verb following it, forms a verbal noun, here meaning "his rage"). The meaning is: let him picture in his own mind that if he does this, will the help of Allah that enrages him go away? He called his act a "scheme" sarcastically, because he did not scheme against the one he envies; rather, he schemed against himself. The intended meaning is: he has in his power nothing that can remove what enrages him.

﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾: like that sending down, He sent down the entire Qur'an, ﴿as clear signs﴾, evident and manifest, ﴿and that Allah guides whom He wills﴾. That is: and because Allah guides by it those whom He knows will believe, or He makes firm those who believed and increases them in guidance, He sent it down in this way, made clear.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners (with Allah)﴾ It is said: the religions are five: four belong to Satan and one belongs to the Most Merciful. The Sabians are a type of Christians, so they are not counted as six. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ in their states and their places, so He does not requite them with one single recompense, nor gather them in one single station. The predicate of ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ and ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ is like when you say, "Indeed Zayd, indeed his father is standing." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things﴾: He knows them and preserves them. So let every person look to his belief, his statement, and his action. And this is the most eloquent warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 18:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ — meaning: Have you not known, O Muhammad, with a knowledge that stands in place of direct sight — ﴿that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, and the creatures﴾. It has been said that all of them prostrate to Him, but we do not perceive this, just as we do not perceive their glorification (tasbih). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it exalts Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra: 44]. It has also been said that the compliance of a non-accountable being (ghayr al-mukallaf) with Him in what occurs to it of His acts and His subjugation of it is called prostration to Him, by way of likening its compliance to the prostration of the accountable being, beneath which every act of submission falls short.

﴿And many of (p-433) mankind﴾ — that is: and many of mankind prostrate to Him in the prostration of obedience and worship. Or it is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿of mankind﴾ being a qualifier of it, and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, which is ﴿is rewarded﴾ (muthab). This is indicated by His words ﴿and many have the punishment justly due against them﴾, meaning: and many of them have the punishment justly due against them, because of their disbelief and their refusal to prostrate.

﴿And whoever Allah humiliates﴾ with wretchedness, ﴿for him there is no honorer﴾ with felicity. ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ of honoring and humiliating and other things. The apparent meaning of this verse and the one before it refutes the Mu'tazilah's view, for they say that He willed things and did not do them, whereas He says: ﴿He does what He wills﴾.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 19:

﴿These two are two adversaries (khasmān)﴾, i.e., two opposing groups (farīqān mukhtasimān). Al-khaṣm (the adversary) is an attribute by which the group is described. His words ﴿disputed (ikhtaṣamū)﴾ are in accordance with the meaning (li-l-ma'nā), while ﴿these two (hādhān)﴾ is in accordance with the wording (li-l-lafẓ). The intended meaning is the believers and the disbelievers.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it refers back to the people of the religions mentioned, so the believers and the rest of the five are one adversary (khaṣm) ﴿concerning their Lord﴾, i.e., concerning His religion and His attributes. Then he explained the recompense of each adversary by His words ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾, and this is the decisive judgment (faṣl al-khuṣūma) meant by His words ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 17]. ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾: as if Allah decrees for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enveloping them, just as worn garments are cut. The past tense is chosen because it is certain to occur without doubt, so it is like the established and realized. ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾: with the kasra of the hā' and the mīm, Baṣrī reads it; with the ḍamma, Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Khalaf read it; and with the kasra of the hā' and the ḍamma of the mīm, the others read it. ﴿al-ḥamīm﴾ is the hot water. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: if a single drop of it fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 20:

﴿Yuṣhharu﴾ means it is melted (yudhābu) ﴿bihi﴾ by the boiling water (al-ḥamīm), ﴿mā fī buṭūnihim wal-julūd﴾: that is, it melts their intestines and their insides just as it melts their skins, so it affects both the outward and the inward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 21:

﴿And for them are maqami'* (rods)﴾ whips specific to them, ﴿of iron﴾, with which they are beaten.

*Maqami' (مَقامِع): plural of miqma'a (مِقْمَعَة), an implement used for striking and restraining, here understood as a whip or rod of iron.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 22:

﴿Whenever they wish to come out of it﴾ from the Fire ﴿out of distress﴾. The phrase "min ghammin" is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for "minha," either by repeating the preposition, or the first "min" denotes the starting point of the motion (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), while the second means "out of" (min ajl). That is: whenever they wish to come out of the Fire out of distress that overtakes them, they are brought out, ﴿they are returned to it﴾ with the maqami' (iron hooks/maces). According to al-Hasan, the meaning of "coming out" is that the Fire strikes them with its flames and throws them to its upper part, then they are struck with the maqami' and they fall back into it for seventy autumns. The intended meaning is that they are returned to the main body of the Fire, not that they are fully separated from it and then return to it. ﴿And taste﴾ i.e., it is said to them: taste ﴿the punishment of the Burning﴾, which is the intense, widespread fire of great destructiveness.

Then he mentioned the reward of the other party, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets﴾ (asāwir), the plural of (siwār) in the plural of (aswira), ﴿of gold and pearls﴾. Al-Madani and ʿAsim read "pearls" in the accusative, on the basis of "and they will be given" (wa yu'tūna), while the others read it in the genitive, coordinating it with "of gold." Abu Bakr and Hammad omit the first hamza throughout the Qur'an. ﴿And their clothing therein will be silk﴾ (ḥarīr), which is brocade (ibrīsam).

And they were guided to the good word and were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy. That is: in this world they were guided to the word of tawhid (monotheism) and to the path of the Praiseworthy, meaning Islam. Or, in the Hereafter, God inspired them to say, "Praise belongs to God, who has made His promise true to us," and guided them to the way of Paradise. And al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy) is God, who is praised by every tongue.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ means: they prevent [people] from entering Islam. "And bar" (wa-yaṣuddūn) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "disbelieve," meaning: while they bar [others]. The barring from them is constant and continuous, just as one says, "So-and-so does good to the poor," where what is meant is the continuity of the existence of this doing of good from him, in the present and in the future. ﴿And [from] the Sacred Mosque﴾ means: and they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque and from entering it, ﴿which We have made for mankind﴾ absolutely, without any distinction between the resident and the visitor from the desert (al-bād). If by "the Sacred Mosque" is meant Makkah, then in this there is evidence that the houses of Makkah may not be sold. If by it is meant the House (al-Bayt), then the meaning is that it is a qiblah for all people. "Equal" (sawā'an), with the accusative, is read by Ḥafṣ, as a second object of "We made it," meaning: We made it equal. ﴿The one who dwells therein and the visitor﴾. "Ghayr al-muqīm" with the yā' is read by Makkī, and Abū 'Amr agreed with him in connected speech; the others read it with the nominative, as a predicate, with the subject postponed, meaning: the one who dwells therein and the visitor are equal, and the clause is the second object, while "for mankind" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿And whoever intends therein﴾ — in the Sacred Mosque — ﴿with deviation, with injustice﴾: these are two synonymous circumstantial clauses, and the object of "intends" is omitted so that it may encompass every possible object, as if he said: whoever intends therein any intention, deviating from the right course and unjust. Thus "deviation" (ilḥād) is turning away from the right course. ﴿We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾ — a painful punishment in the Hereafter. The predicate of "indeed" (inna) is omitted, the answer of the conditional indicating it, its estimated form being: Indeed those who disbelieve and bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque — We will make them taste a painful punishment; and everyone who commits a sin therein is likewise.

﴿And [remember] when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾. Say, O Muhammad: remember when We made the place of the House a return (mabāʼah) for Abraham, meaning a place to which he would return for its building and for worship (ʿibādah). The House had been raised up to the heavens at the time of the Flood, and it was made of a red ruby. God informed Abraham of its place by sending a wind that swept clear the site of the House, so he built it on its ancient foundation (ʾussih al-qadīm).

﴿An﴾ is the explanatory (mufassirah) particle for an implied saying, meaning: saying to him, ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols and filth. Madani (the Medinan reader) and Ḥafṣ read the yāʼ with a fatḥah, [as in بَيْتِيَ]. ﴿For those who circumambulate﴾ it, ﴿and those who stand﴾ and reside in Mecca, ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning those who pray. The words rākiʻ and sājid are plural forms (jamʻ) of rākiʻ and sājid.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 27:

﴿And proclaim to the people the Pilgrimage﴾ (wa-adhdhin fi al-nas bil-hajj): call out among them. The ḥajj (pilgrimage) is the emphatic intention to a noble destination. It is related that he climbed Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord," and those who were destined to make the pilgrimage from the loins and wombs answered: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am." It is also related from al-Hasan that it is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was commanded to do this during the Farewell Pilgrimage. The first view is more apparent. The response to the command is ﴿They will come to you on foot﴾ (ya'tuka rijalan): mushāt (on foot), the plural of rājil, like qā'im and qiyām. ﴿And upon every lean camel﴾ (wa-ʿala kulli ḍāmir): a circumstantial clause conjoined to "rijālan," as if he had said: on foot and riding. The ḍāmir is the emaciated camel. The men are mentioned before the riders to show the virtue of those who walk, as is found in the hadith. ﴿They will come﴾ (ya'tīna): an attribute of kulli ḍāmir, because it has the meaning of a plural. ʿAbd Allah recited "ya'tūna," as an attribute of al-rijal and al-rukban. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾ (min kulli fajjin): a path; ﴿far-off﴾ (ʿamīq): distant. Muhammad ibn Yasin said: An elderly man said to me during the circumambulation, "Where are you from?" I said, "From Khurasan." He said, "How far are you from the House?" I said, "A journey of two or three months." He said, "Then you are neighbours of the House." I said, "Where have you come from?" He said, "From a journey of five years. I set out when I was young and have grown old." I said, "By Allah, this is a beautiful obedience and a sincere love." He laughed and said:

Visit the one you love, though the distance between you is far and veils and curtains stand between you.

Let not distance keep you from visiting him; the lover is always a visitor to the one he loves.

The lam in ﴿لِيَشْهَدُوا﴾ (li-yashhadū), meaning "so that they may attend" (li-yahduru), is connected to ﴿أذِّنْ﴾ (adhdhin, "proclaim") or to ﴿يَأْتُوكَ﴾ (ya'tūka, "they will come to you"). ﴿Manāfi'a lahum﴾ ("benefits for them") is indefinite (nakkarahā), because he intended benefits specific to this worship, both religious and worldly, which are not found in other acts of worship. This is because worship is legislated as a trial of the self, as in prayer and fasting, or a trial of wealth, as in zakat. The Hajj includes both, along with bearing hardships, facing dangers, leaving behind means and severing ties with friends, leaving cities and homelands, and separation from children and companions. It also serves as a reminder of what continues when a person moves from the abode of perishing to the abode of permanence. The pilgrim who enters the desert relies only on his provisions and eats only from his own supplies, and so too is the person who leaves the shore of life and boards the sea of death: nothing benefits his loneliness except what he strove for in his livelihood for his afterlife, and nothing comforts his loneliness except the litanies he used to find comfort in. The washing of the one who enters the state of ihram, his preparation, his wearing of unstitched garments, and his perfuming are a mirror of what will happen to him: being placed on his bier for washing and preparation, perfumed with hanut (camphor-based perfume), and wrapped in an unstitched shroud. Then the muhrim (one in ihram) is disheveled and bewildered, and likewise on the Day of Resurrection he will come forth from the grave in dread. The standing of the pilgrims at 'Arafat, hoping with desire and fear, asking with hope and dread, while among them are the accepted and the rejected, is like the standing of the plains of judgment: ﴿No soul shall speak except by His permission; then among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾ [Hud: 105]. The departure to Muzdalifah in the evening is the driving toward the decision of judgment, and Mina is the place of hope for the sinners awaiting the intercession of the interceders. Shaving the head and cleanliness are like emerging from sins through mercy and lightening. The Sacred House, whoever enters it is safe from harm and fighting, is a model of the Abode of Peace, whoever enters it remains safe from annihilation and extinction. Yet Paradise is surrounded by the disliked things of the self, just as the Ka'bah is surrounded by the destructive dangers of the desert. So welcome to whoever crosses the deadly deserts, longing for the meeting on the Day of Calling (yawm al-tanād). ﴿And that they may mention the name of God﴾ at the slaughter ﴿on known days﴾ — these are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, and the last of them is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and of most of the exegetes, may God have mercy on them. According to his two companions, they are the days of sacrifice (ayyām al-nahr), which is the view of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both. ﴿Over what He has provided them of the livestock beasts﴾ — that is, over slaughtering them — and this supports their view. The word bahīmah refers to any four-legged animal, on land or sea, and it is specified by al-an'ām, which are camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. ﴿So eat from them﴾ — from their meat. The imperative here indicates permission (li-l-ibāḥah). It is permissible to eat from the voluntary offering (hady al-taṭawwu'), and from the offering of tamattu' and qiran, because it is a sacrifice of ritual worship (dam nusuk), resembling the udhiyah (sacrificial offering). It is not permissible to eat from the remaining offerings. ﴿And feed the distressed poor﴾ — the one afflicted by bu's, meaning hardship; "the needy" — the one whose poverty has weakened him.

﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness﴾: then let them remove from themselves their dirt (adran). So said Nifṭawayh. It was said that the ending of the tafath (the dirt or unkemptness of the pilgrim's body, the residue of the state of ihram) is trimming the moustache and the nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair (al-istihdad). The intended meaning is the removal of the tafath. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: the ending of the tafath is all the rites of the Hajj.

﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾: the obligations of their Hajj. The Arabs say of anyone who fulfils what was incumbent upon him, "he fulfilled his vow," even if he had not vowed. Or it means the acts of righteousness that they vow to perform during their Hajj. "Wa-liyuwaffū" with a sukun on the lam and a shadda (on the fa), is the reading of Abu Bakr.

﴿And let them circumambulate﴾: the Tawaf al-Ziyarah (the circumambulation of visitation, the pillar of the Hajj), by which the complete exit from the state of ihram (tahallul) is achieved. The three lams (of the three imperatives) are read with a sukun according to all except Ibn ʿAyyash and Abu ʿAmr.

﴿The Ancient House﴾: the old one, because it is the first house set up for mankind, built by Adam and then renewed by Ibrahim. Or "al-ʿatiq" means "the noble," from ʿitāq al-khayl (the noble horses), for their excellence, and ʿitāq al-raqīq (the freeing of slaves), because it [the House] brought its people out of the humiliation of servitude to the nobility of freedom. Or it is so called because it was freed (ʿutiqa) from drowning, for it was raised up during the time of the Flood. Or it was freed from the hands of tyrants, for how many a tyrant set out towards it to demolish it, and God prevented him. Or it was freed from the hands of owners, so it was never owned. It is the place of circumambulation for the people of the earth, just as the Throne is the place of circumambulation for the people of the heavens. When the seeker is stirred by the company of longing and drawn by the attractions of desire, he begins to cross the shoulders of the earth in stages and takes the paths of perils as lodgings. When he beholds the House, the consolation of it only increases his yearning, and the healing of touching the Black Stone only gives him more burning. Thus grief makes him restless, lamenting, and longing sends him back and forth around it in circling.

The tawaf al-ziyarah is the last of the three pillars of the Hajj, and the first of them is ihram, which is a binding contract resembling holding fast to the handhold of Islam, so that it does not come undone through committing what is forbidden in it, and its contract remains despite what would corrupt or contradict it, just as the contract of Islam is not dissolved by the crowding of sins, and a thousand sins are lifted by one repentance. The second is standing at ʿArafat, with the mark of supplication, in the manner of earnest concern, and sincere withdrawal from relying on the ranks of deeds and the evidence of states.

(p. 439) **﴿Dhalika﴾** (*dhalika*, "that") is the predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence) of an elided subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence). The sense is: "The matter is that," or its implied meaning is: "They should do that." **﴿And whoever honours the sacred things of Allah﴾**: a *hurmah* (sacred thing) is that which may not be violated. All that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has imposed on the servant with this quality, such as the rites of the Hajj and others, is included. It may be general, covering all of His obligations, or it may be specific to what concerns the Hajj. It has also been said that "the sacred things of Allah" are the Sacred House, the Sacred Monument, the Sacred Month, the Sacred Land, and the Sacred Mosque. **﴿Then it is better for him with his Lord﴾**: *dhalika* ("it") refers to the honouring. The meaning of honouring (*ta'zim*) is knowing that these things must be observed, guarded, and upheld. **﴿And the livestock has been made lawful for you﴾**, meaning all of it, **﴿except what is recited to you﴾**, that is, the verse forbidding it, which is His saying: **﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾** (Qur'an 5:3), and so on. The meaning is: Allah, the Exalted, made all livestock lawful for you except what He explained in His Book. So observe His limits, and do not forbid anything that has been made lawful, such as the forbidding by some of the *bahirah* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released) and similar practices. Nor make lawful what He has forbidden, such as their permitting the eating of the *mawqudhah* (an animal killed by a blow) and the carrion and others.

When He had urged the honouring of His sacred things, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, by His saying: **﴿So avoid the filth of idols, and avoid the word of falsehood﴾** (Qur'an 22:30), because that is among the greatest and foremost of sacred things. **﴿Of idols﴾** (*min al-awthan*) is an explanation (*bayan*, an explicative clause) of **﴿the filth﴾** (*al-rijs*), because *al-rijs* is unspecified and applies to many things, as if it were said: "Avoid the filth, which is idols." He called idols "filth" by way of comparison, meaning: you recoil from filth by your natures, so you must recoil from them as well.

He combined *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) with **﴿the word of falsehood﴾**, that is, lying and slander, or false testimony. It derives from *zawar*, which means deviation, because *shirk* is a kind of falsehood, since the polytheist claims that the idol has a right to be worshipped.

﴿Ḥunafāʾa lillāh﴾ (ḥunafāʾ, "upright in faith"): Muslims, ﴿not associating [anything] with Him﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a grammatical term for a phrase describing the state of the subject) parallel to ﴿ḥunafāʾ﴾. ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen﴾ (kharra), meaning dropped, ﴿from the sky﴾ to the earth, ﴿and the birds snatch him away﴾, meaning they carry him off swiftly. The reading ﴿fa-takhaṭṭafahu﴾ (with the doubled tāʾ) is that of Madani (a reader of the Qur'an, one of the canonical or accepted reciters from Medina). ﴿Or the wind throws him down﴾, meaning it causes him to fall, ﴿into a far-off place﴾ (saḥīq), meaning distant.

(p-٤٤٠) Al-Hawī means falling.

This may be a compound simile (tashbīh murakkab), or it may be a set of separate similes (tashbīh mufarraq). If it is a compound simile, the meaning is: whoever associates partners with Allah has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, since his condition is depicted as the condition of one who falls from the sky, and the birds seize him and tear him into pieces in their crops, or the wind sweeps him away until it throws him into some distant places of destruction. If it is a set of separate similes, then faith in its loftiness is likened to the sky, the one who associates partners with Allah to the one who falls from the sky, the destructive desires (al-ahwāʾ al-murdiya) to the various birds, and Satan, who causes him to go astray, to the wind that hurls what it sweeps up into some of the ruinous pits.

ذَلِكَ — that is the matter (lit. "that," i.e., the matter is so).

﴿وَمَن يُعَظِّمْ شَعَائِرَ اللَّهِ﴾ — "And whoever honors the rites of Allah." Glorifying the rites (sha'a'ir) is what is meant here, and the sha'a'ir are the sacrificial animals (al-hada_ya, the offerings), because they are among the markers (ma'alim) of the Hajj: one chooses them to be large in body, fine, fat, and high in price.

﴿فَإِنَّهَا مِن تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ﴾ — "For indeed it is from the piety of hearts." That is: indeed, glorifying them is among the actions of those who possess piety of the heart. The phrases ("those who possess") have been elided, and "the hearts" is mentioned because they are the seats of piety.

For you there are benefits in them (of riding when needed and drinking their milk when necessary) until a specified term, (that is) until they are slaughtered. Then their place of sacrifice (i.e., the time when it becomes obligatory to slaughter them) is at the Ancient House. What is meant is that they are slaughtered in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), which has the ruling of the House, since the Haram is the protected surroundings of the House. A similar extension is in your saying, "I reached the city," while in fact your journey only reached its boundaries. It was also said that "the rites" (al-sha'a'ir) means all the rites of pilgrimage (al-manasik), and "glorifying them" means completing them; but "their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House" rejects this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 22, verse 34:

﴿And for every community﴾, a believing congregation before you, ﴿We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. As for the word "ḥaythu" here: ʿAlī and Ḥamzah read the vowel of the sīn in مَنسَكًا as kasra (i.e. مِنسَكًا), meaning "place" (mawḍiʿ), that is, the place of sacrifice (mawḍiʿ qurbān). The others read it with a fatḥa, as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning the shedding of blood and the slaughtering of offerings. ﴿That they may mention the name of Allah﴾, alone and to the exclusion of any other, ﴿over what He has provided for them of the cattle of grazing animals﴾, that is, at the time of their sacrificing and slaughtering them. (p-441) ﴿So your God is one God﴾, meaning: mention the name of Allah alone over the slaughter, for your God is one God. In this is evidence that mentioning the name of Allah is a condition of slaughter. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, prescribed for every community that they perform the rite (yansukū) for Him, that is, that they slaughter for Him seeking nearness to Him, and He made the reason for this that His name be mentioned over the sacrificial animals — exalted are His names. His words ﴿So to Him submit﴾ mean: devote the remembrance to Him exclusively, and make it wholly His (sāliman), that is, pure, without mixing it with any associating of partners. ﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitīn)﴾, those who are at peace (al-muṭmaʾinnīn) in the remembrance of Allah, or the humble and submissive (al-khāshiʿīn), from al-khabt, which is the low-lying, level ground of the earth. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are those who do not wrong, and when they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.
